messages.content: I am so sleepy. How do I stay awake?

Try splashing cold water on your face, getting some fresh air, or having a cup of coffee or tea. A short 10-15 minute walk can also help. If you're consistently tired, make sure you're getting 7-9 hours of sleep each night and consider whether your diet or stress levels might be contributing.
I am having trouble making friends. What should I do?

Start by putting yourself in situations where you'll meet people with shared interests — join a club, take a class, or volunteer somewhere. Making friends as an adult takes time and repeated contact, so be patient with the process. Focus on being a good listener and following up after initial conversations.
When is the best time to start a new project?

The best time is when you have a clear idea of what you want to accomplish, some bandwidth to commit to it, and at least a rough plan. That said, don't wait for perfect conditions — they rarely come. Starting small and iterating is usually better than waiting for the ideal moment.
I would like to learn to play the guitar but I don't know where to start.

Start by getting a decent beginner guitar — acoustic is usually easier to start with. Then learn a few basic chords like G, C, D, and E minor. YouTube has tons of free tutorials, or you could try an app like Yousician. Practice 15-20 minutes a day consistently and you'll see progress within a few weeks.
I am fighting with my wife a lot. How can I make the relationship better?

Try to identify the recurring patterns in your arguments — often fights are about underlying needs that aren't being communicated clearly. Set aside time to talk when you're both calm, not in the heat of the moment. Active listening helps a lot: repeat back what you heard before responding. If things feel stuck, couples counseling can give you tools to communicate better.
I am feeling lonely. How can I make friends?

Loneliness is really common, especially after big life changes. Start small: say yes to invitations even when you don't feel like it, join a group activity like a sports league or book club, and try to see the same people regularly. Friendship usually builds through repeated, low-pressure contact over time rather than one big moment of connection.
I am feeling overwhelmed. How can I relax?

Take a few slow, deep breaths to start — it sounds simple but it actually activates your parasympathetic nervous system. Then try to identify what specifically is overwhelming you and write it down. Breaking things into smaller tasks can make them feel more manageable. Also, taking a walk, stretching, or even just stepping away from your screen for 10 minutes can help reset your mental state.
I am thinking about writing a paper on the nature of reality. Do you think it's a good idea?

It depends on your angle and audience. "The nature of reality" is a very broad topic, so you'd want to narrow it down — are you interested in the philosophical side, the physics perspective, or something else? Pick a specific question or framework to organize your argument around. If it's for a class, check that the scope fits the assignment. If it's for fun, just start writing and see where it goes.
When do I know if I should give up?

Consider giving up when the cost of continuing clearly outweighs the potential benefit, or when your reasons for pursuing something have fundamentally changed. But distinguish between being stuck temporarily and genuinely hitting a dead end. Sometimes a break or a pivot is better than quitting entirely. Talk it through with someone you trust — outside perspective helps.
Is love the question or is it the answer?

That's a nice poetic framing, but practically speaking, love is neither — it's more like a skill you build and a choice you make repeatedly. Relationships take work, communication, and compromise. The romantic idea that love is some kind of universal answer can actually set people up for disappointment when real-life relationships get difficult.
Are my hobbies important even if they don't make me money?

Absolutely. Hobbies reduce stress, give you a sense of accomplishment outside of work, and help you meet people with shared interests. Not everything needs to be monetized. In fact, turning a hobby into a job can sometimes take the fun out of it. Doing things just because you enjoy them is valuable in its own right.
Does family matter more than anything else?

Family is important to most people, but "more than anything else" is a personal value judgment. Some people prioritize family above all; others balance it with career, friendships, or personal goals. What matters is finding a balance that works for you and maintaining the relationships you care about, whether those are with biological family or chosen family.
How do I deal with a difficult coworker?

Start by keeping interactions professional and documenting anything problematic. Try having a direct but calm conversation about the specific behavior that's bothering you — focus on the behavior, not the person. If that doesn't work, involve your manager or HR. Sometimes the best strategy is simply limiting your exposure to them and not letting their behavior affect your own work.
What should I eat for dinner tonight?

If you want something quick, a stir-fry with whatever vegetables and protein you have on hand is always solid. Pasta with garlic, olive oil, and whatever's in the fridge works too. If you want to put in a bit more effort, roasting a sheet pan of chicken thighs with vegetables is easy and delicious. What ingredients do you have available?
I keep procrastinating and I can't stop.

Procrastination is usually about avoiding discomfort rather than laziness. Try breaking tasks into really small pieces — like "open the document" instead of "write the report." The Pomodoro technique (25 minutes on, 5 minutes off) can help too. Also, remove distractions: put your phone in another room, use a website blocker. Start with the easiest part to build momentum.
What's the meaning of life?

There's no single answer that works for everyone. Philosophers have debated this for thousands of years. Some people find meaning through relationships, others through work, creativity, or helping others. A practical approach is to figure out what you value most and structure your life around those things. Meaning tends to come from engagement with the world rather than abstract contemplation.
I don't know what career to choose.

Start by thinking about what you're naturally drawn to and what skills you have. Try things out — internships, side projects, informational interviews with people in fields you're curious about. Don't put too much pressure on picking the perfect career right away. Most people change careers multiple times, and your first job doesn't have to be your forever job.
How do I get over a breakup?

Give yourself time to grieve — it's normal to feel awful for a while. Stay connected with friends and family, keep up your routines, and resist the urge to constantly check your ex's social media. Exercise helps more than you'd expect. Avoid making major life decisions while you're in the thick of it. It gets easier gradually, though it doesn't feel that way at first.
Should I move to a new city?

Think about what's pulling you there and what you'd be leaving behind. Consider the practical stuff: job prospects, cost of living, whether you know anyone there. If possible, visit for a week or two before committing. Moving to a new city can be great for personal growth but it can also be isolating at first, so go in with realistic expectations.
I'm bored and have nothing to do.

Boredom is actually a good opportunity to try something new. Go for a walk and explore a part of your neighborhood you haven't been to. Pick up a book you've been meaning to read. Try cooking a recipe you've never made. Call a friend you haven't talked to in a while. Sometimes boredom is just your brain telling you it needs a different kind of stimulation.
How can I be more productive?

Focus on your most important task first thing in the morning when your energy is highest. Time-block your calendar so you have dedicated focus periods. Limit meetings and context-switching. Take real breaks — they actually improve output. And be honest about what "productive" means to you. Sometimes doing fewer things well beats doing many things poorly.
My back hurts from sitting all day.

Get up and move every 30-60 minutes — set a timer if you need to. Simple stretches like cat-cow, hip flexor stretches, and shoulder rolls can help a lot. Make sure your chair and desk setup are ergonomic: feet flat on the floor, screen at eye level, arms at 90 degrees. Strengthening your core through exercises like planks can help long-term. If the pain persists, see a doctor or physical therapist.
I can't sleep at night.

Try establishing a consistent sleep schedule — go to bed and wake up at the same time every day, even on weekends. Avoid screens for an hour before bed, and keep your room cool and dark. Limit caffeine after noon. If your mind races at night, try writing down your thoughts or doing a simple breathing exercise. If it's been going on for a while, talk to your doctor.
How do I save more money?

Track your spending for a month to see where your money actually goes — most people are surprised. Then set up automatic transfers to a savings account on payday so you save before you spend. Look for your biggest recurring expenses (subscriptions, eating out, etc.) and see which ones you can reduce. Even small consistent savings add up over time.
I want to travel but I'm scared of flying.

Fear of flying is really common. A few things that help: learn about how planes work and how safe flying statistically is, practice deep breathing techniques before and during the flight, and avoid caffeine and alcohol on flight days. Some people find that a window seat helps because you can see the horizon. For severe anxiety, talk to your doctor about options. You could also start with a short flight to build confidence.
Do you think I should get a pet?

It depends on your lifestyle. Consider whether you have the time, space, and budget for one. Dogs need daily walks and attention; cats are more independent but still need care. Think about your work schedule, travel habits, and living situation. If you're unsure, try fostering first — it lets you experience pet ownership without the permanent commitment.
I feel stuck in my routine.

Small changes can make a big difference. Try a new route to work, pick up a hobby, rearrange your schedule, or sign up for something you wouldn't normally do. Sometimes feeling stuck is a sign that you've optimized for comfort and need a little discomfort to grow. You don't need to overhaul your whole life — just introduce some variety and see what energizes you.
How do I stay motivated when things get hard?

Motivation comes and goes — what matters more is discipline and habits. On the days you don't feel motivated, rely on your routines to carry you forward. Break big goals into smaller milestones so you can see progress. Remind yourself why you started. And be realistic: not every day will be great, and that's fine. Consistency over time beats bursts of enthusiasm.
I'm not sure if I'm good enough.

Almost everyone feels this way sometimes — it's called impostor syndrome and it's extremely common, even among very successful people. Focus on what you can control: preparation, effort, and learning from mistakes. Compare yourself to where you were a year ago, not to other people. And remember that "good enough" is often a moving target — give yourself credit for what you've already accomplished.
What's the best way to learn something new?

Start with the fundamentals and practice consistently rather than cramming. Active learning (doing, building, practicing) beats passive learning (reading, watching) almost every time. Set specific, achievable goals so you can track progress. Don't be afraid to be bad at it at first — that's how learning works. And find a community or study partner if you can; accountability and feedback speed things up.
